extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and their attorneys/agents
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards from the MPEP for suggesting, searching, requiring, and handling patent interferences (including applicant- and examiner-suggested interferences, priority showings, claim-sorting, file control, and related statutory limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to suggest interference (timing/ties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences between two applications should be extremely rare; suspensions must not be used to create ties. If two applications are ready to issue and have earliest effective filing dates within six months of each other, an interference may be suggested. If one application's earliest effective filing date is more than six months before the other's, the earlier application should issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating artificial ties by suspension. If the earlier application is available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e) against the later application, make a rejection instead of suggesting interference. If not, require a showing of priority under 37 CFR 41.202(d). See MPEP § 2305.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve outstanding proceedings before suggesting interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents/applications that are subject to other proceedings (e.g., reexamination, reissue, petitions to accept late maintenance fees, requests for disclaimers or corrections) must have those issues resolved before an interference is suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such outstanding issues may affect whether or how an interference may be declared. For example, if a maintenance fee petition is denied and the patent is expired, an interference cannot be declared. Ensure all relevant proceedings (including corrections and reissues that change claims) are concluded or addressed first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expired patent cannot be part of an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference cannot be declared with an expired patent (e.g., patent expired for failure to timely pay maintenance fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a petition to accept delayed maintenance payment (37 CFR 1.378) is not granted and the patent remains expired by operation of law (35 U.S.C. 41(b)), do not declare an interference. Use example guidance provided in the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference not declared between two patents
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference may not be declared between two patents (35 U.S.C. 135(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim of an application interferes with a claim of an issued patent, do not allow the application claim to issue; instead suggest an interference. The interfering claim in the application should be held from issuance and handled as an interference matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer or correction removing common claim eliminates interference
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclaimer under 35 U.S.C. 253 or a correction under 35 U.S.C. 254/255 changes a patent claim such that it no longer is directed to the same invention as the other party's claims, no interference can be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes that remove the common subject matter remove the basis for an interference; other rejections (e.g., double-patenting) may still be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of inventorship can eliminate interference
rubrics_metrics.description: If inventorship is corrected so that the inventors for the patent and the application are the same, the interference basis under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1) (which requires 'another inventor') is eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where inventorship correction removes the 'another inventor' requirement, consider other rejections as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may suggest an interference and required consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference suggestion may come from an applicant or an examiner. Whoever suggests it determines what must be done prior to declaration. In either case the examiner must consult with an Interference Practice Specialist (IPS), who may refer the suggestion to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should involve the IPS early; the IPS may require memoranda or participation in conferences with the Board before referral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference search requirement (when app is in condition for allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is in condition for allowance, an interference search must be performed by text searching the 'US-PGPUB' database in EAST or WEST directed to the comprehensive inventive features in the broadest claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims involve nucleotide or peptide sequences, request STIC to perform a sequence interference search. Make a printout of the database(s) searched, the query(ies) used, and the date of the search of record in the application file; do NOT place the search results in the application file. The search must extend beyond the application's class/subclass to all relevant classes and Technology Centers (see MPEP § 1302.08).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain control over involved files / file availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications believed to interfere should ordinarily be assigned to the same examiner. All relevant files (including paper benefit files and PCT files when required) must be available before referring a suggested interference to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applications are in different Technology Centers, reassign one so both are in the TC where the commonly claimed invention would be classified. Reconstruct lost paper file wrappers before referral. Obtain PCT files when benefit is claimed solely to the PCT application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified translation required for foreign benefit applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A certified English translation of every foreign benefit application or PCT application not filed in English is required to accord benefit (35 U.S.C. 119(b)(3), 372(b)(3); 37 CFR 1.55(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no certified translation is in the official record, require the applicant to file one; reliance on a non-English application is prima facie insufficient without a certified translation (37 CFR 41.154(b), 41.202(e)). Use Form Paragraph 23.19 to notify applicant when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorting claims / consolidating interfering claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant has several related applications with interfering claims intermixed with non-interfering claims, the examiner should consider consolidating interfering claims into a single application or restricting an application to non-interfering claims so examination can proceed for non-interfering claims without interference delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interfering claims are 'conflicting claims' under 37 CFR 1.78(b); the examiner may require consolidation into any applicant disclosure that supports the claims (35 U.S.C. 132(a)). Alternatively require restriction so applicant can file a divisional for non-interfering claims (35 U.S.C. 121). Do not consolidate a claim into an application lacking 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support for that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant suggestion formal requirements (37 CFR 41.202(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion must provide sufficient information to identify the application or patent with which the applicant seeks an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually providing the serial or patent number suffices. If the applicant only has indirect evidence (journal notice, 'patent pending', foreign publication), provide likely inventors/assignees to aid the examiner in identifying the other application; inadequate identification may prevent declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant requirement to identify all interfering claims, propose counts, and show correspondence (37 CFR 41.202(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestion must identify all claims the applicant believes interfere, propose one or more counts, and show how the claims correspond to one or more counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A count is a description of the interfering subject matter used by the Board to determine what evidence may prove priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g)(1). The applicant must identify at least one patentable claim from every application or patent that interferes for each count.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each count provide claim chart comparing at least one claim of each party (37 CFR 41.202(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: For each proposed count, the suggestion must include a claim chart comparing at least one claim of each party corresponding to the count and show why the claims interfere within the meaning of § 41.203(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must confirm that (A) at least one patentable count is identified, (B) at least one patentable claim from each party is identified for each count, and (C) a claim chart comparing at least one set of claims for each count is provided. The examiner need not agree with the applicant's suggestion but must check formal compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must explain in detail why it will prevail on priority (37 CFR 41.202(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must explain in detail why it would prevail on priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the applicant's earliest constructive reduction-to-practice is later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice of the other party, the applicant must show why it would prevail. Failure to do so may still result in an interference declaration to place the applicant under an order to show cause; new evidence is limited except for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim added/amended to provoke interference must include written-description claim chart (37 CFR 41.202(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim has been added or amended to provoke an interference, the applicant must provide a claim chart showing the written description for each claim in the applicant's specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because added or amended claims copied from an opponent may lack equivalent written description support in the applicant's disclosure, such claims are subject to heightened scrutiny early in the interference (see 'Threshold issue' under 37 CFR 41.201). Use Form Paragraph 23.06.05 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charts for claimed constructive reductions-to-practice (37 CFR 41.202(a)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: For each constructive reduction-to-practice for which the applicant wishes to be accorded benefit, provide a chart showing where the disclosure provides a constructive reduction-to-practice within the scope of the interfering subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description in an application that would have anticipated the subject matter of a count is a constructive reduction-to-practice. One disclosed embodiment can suffice. For benefit chains under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/121/365 the anticipating disclosure must be continuously disclosed through the entire benefit chain or no benefit is accorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner review of applicant suggestion: formal sufficiency vs substantive adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant suggests an interference under 37 CFR 41.202(a), the examiner must review the suggestion for formal sufficiency but is generally not responsible for determining the substantive adequacy of any priority showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner may, however, offer pertinent observations on any showing when the suggestion is referred to the Board; such observations may be attached to Form PTO-850. Use form paragraphs 23.06–23.06.06 to acknowledge and specify deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive reduction-to-practice and priority evidence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant's constructive reduction-to-practice is earlier than the other's apparent earliest, applicant may simply explain entitlement; otherwise the applicant must (A) antedate the other's constructive reduction-to-practice, (B) demonstrate why the other is not entitled to its apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice, or (C) provide some other reason why the applicant should be considered the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showings may resemble those under 37 CFR 1.130–1.132 but differ in scope. The chain-of-benefit rule requires continuous disclosure. Where evidence or testimony necessary to show priority is unavailable without authorization, the showing must include interrogatories, requests for production, depositions, and a detailed proffer of expected responses and their relevance (see 37 CFR 41.154(b) and 41.202(d)/(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: If suggestion used instead of 37 CFR 1.130–1.132 declaration, check 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/102(e) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant files a suggestion under 37 CFR 41.202(a) instead of a declaration under 37 CFR 1.130–1.132, and an application claim is subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or 102(e), the examiner must verify that the applicant's showing, taken at face value, is sufficient to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner determines the showing is insufficient, examination is not complete (37 CFR 41.102), the rejection should be maintained, and the suggestion should not be referred to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 135(b) (one-year bar and substantially same subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application claim interferes with a patent claim and the applicant added the claim more than one year after the patent's issuance, or the application was filed more than one year after issuance (but the patent is not a statutory bar), an interference will not be declared unless at least one of the claims present in the application or its parent prior to expiration of the one-year period was for 'substantially the same subject matter' as at least one patent claim (35 U.S.C. 135(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is not obviousness but whether all material limitations of the interfering claim necessarily occur in the prior claim (focus on different material limitations). If none of the prior claims meets the 'substantially the same subject matter' test, reject the interfering claim under 35 U.S.C. 135(b) (see In re McGrew). Use form paragraphs 23.14/23.14.01 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate written description for interfering claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is not entitled to an interference simply because it wants one; the interfering claim must be allowable, particularly with respect to the written description supporting the interfering claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims added or amended to provoke an interference are subject to heightened scrutiny for written description adequacy early in the interference (see 37 CFR 41.201 'Threshold issue'). Better practice is to add or amend to a fully supported claim and explain equivalence rather than literally copy an opponent's claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may not directly suggest interference (limited alerting allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot suggest an interference unless it becomes an applicant by filing a reissue application, but may, to the extent permitted under 37 CFR 1.99 and 1.291, alert an examiner to the possibility of an interference in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 1134 and 1901 for permitted communications; a patentee should not use these limited channels to circumvent the rule that only applicants may suggest interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner suggestion must include explanation and Form PTO-850
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner suggests an interference, the suggestion should include an explanation of why at least one claim of every application or patent defines the same invention under 37 CFR 41.203(a). The examiner must also complete Form PTO-850.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should be ready to discuss why claims interfere, whether other claims would be anticipated/obvious if interfering claims are treated as prior art, and entitlement to constructive reductions-to-practice. The IPS may require a memorandum or a conference with the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner may require adding a claim to provoke interference (37 CFR 41.202(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may require an applicant to add a claim to provoke an interference. Failure to satisfy the requirement within the set period (not less than one month) operates as a concession of priority for that subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before requiring a claim, consult with an IPS. The proposed required claim must (1) be patentable to the applicant apart from priority under 35 U.S.C. 102(g), and (2) be drawn to patentable subject matter claimed by another applicant or patentee. The requirement should not be lightly made given the cost/complexity of interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles guiding requiring applicant to add a claim (A–E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guiding principles include: (A) generally do not suggest interference if examination is not otherwise complete; (B) required claim must not encompass prior art or be barred; (C) application must provide adequate 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph support for the required claim; (D) do not require a claim when applicant expressly states the commonly described subject matter is not the applicant's invention; (E) do not require a claim based on a claim from a published application unless that published application's claim has been allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these principles and examples (e.g., prior art, time-bar under 135(b), applicant disclaimers) to exercise discretion. The examiner may withdraw the requirement if persuaded by applicant's reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and consequences for required added claim
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is required, the applicant is given ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS (whichever is longer) to add the claim. Refusal to add the required claim operates as a concession of priority for that subject matter but does not abandon the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provisions of 37 CFR 1.136 do not apply to this time period. If the interference would be with a patent, the applicant must also comply with 37 CFR 41.202(a)(2)–(a)(6). Applicant may respond by identifying an already-existing claim that provides a basis, adding an alternative claim, or explaining why the required claim is not patentable; the examiner may withdraw the requirement if persuaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership limits on declaring interference (37 CFR 41.206)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative patent judge may decline to declare, or may issue judgment in, an interference between an application and another application or patent that are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference is rarely appropriate between claims owned by the same owner. The owner should investigate and elect which application/patent is entitled to priority or otherwise eliminate the need for an interference (cancel claims, disclaim patent claims, amend application claims, or file reissue). If owners disagree, an interference may still be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show priority and sufficiency standards (37 CFR 41.202(d) and (e))
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application has an earliest constructive reduction-to-practice later than the apparent earliest constructive reduction-to-practice of a competing published application with allowed claims or patent, the applicant must make a priority showing under 37 CFR 41.202(d)(1). A showing is not sufficient unless it would, if unrebutted, support a determination of priority in favor of the party making the showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testimony or production necessary to show priority is not available without authorization, the showing must include any necessary interrogatory/request/admission/deposition requests and a detailed proffer of the expected responses and an explanation of relevance. If the applicant fails to show priority, the Board may still declare an interference to place the applicant under an order to show cause; new evidence admission is limited to showings of good cause.
